d.title: Every term in that table is a stage in one loop
d.caption: The glossary reads as fourteen separate ideas and it is really one cycle with named parts. Push an input through the layers, measure how wrong the answer is, send that measurement back through the same layers with the chain rule, and step every weight against its gradient. Everything else in the list — initialisation, normalisation, regularisation, the optimiser, the schedule — is a modification to one of those four stages, which is why each gets its own lesson rather than its own chapter.

nodes.label: Backward
nodes.sub: the chain rule, layer by layer

d.title: Why one rate cannot be right for a whole run
d.caption: The two halves of training want opposite things. Early on the weights are nowhere near a minimum, so a large rate covers ground and the noise of a mini-batch gradient does no harm. Later the same rate makes the optimiser **bounce around the bottom of the valley** without settling, and a smaller one lets it descend. A schedule is the compromise: decide in advance how the rate falls, or let the validation loss decide for you.

nodes.label: So the rate must fall
nodes.sub: on a plan, or on a metric

d.title: Four schedulers, the rate they actually produce
d.caption: Run over a hundred epochs from the same starting rate, the four behave nothing alike. StepLR holds flat and then drops by a factor of ten at a cliff; cosine falls smoothly throughout; OneCycle **starts twenty-five times below the peak**, climbs to it, and then anneals four orders of magnitude below the start. Warm restarts is the odd one — it decays to 6.16e-06 by epoch 29 and jumps straight back to the full rate at epoch 30.

d.title: What warm-up is protecting you from
d.caption: Two things are unreliable at step zero and both feed the same update. Fresh random weights produce large, uninformative gradients, and Adam's second-moment estimate needs a few dozen steps before it means anything — so a full-size rate applied to both can throw the weights somewhere they never recover from, inside the first hundred updates. The fix is to **rise from 0 to the peak over the first 5–10% of steps** and let the statistics settle first.

nodes.label: Adam's v is unreliable
nodes.sub: for the first few dozen steps

d.title: Which schedule, decided by what you know in advance
d.caption: The choice falls out of one question: do you know how long the run is? A known length lets a schedule be planned, and cosine is then the default because it has no hyperparameter beyond that length. An unknown length leaves only the scheduler that reacts to the training itself. The last row applies **whatever** you picked above it.

cells.text: CosineAnnealingLR - no hyperparameters beyond the length
ReduceLROnPlateau - the only one that reacts to training

cells: linear warm-up, then cosine or linear decay
OneCycleLR - super-convergence, if you can tune it

cells.text: warm-up over the first 5-10% of steps, regardless

d.title: The network, with the shape convention stated
d.caption: Two layers — ReLU hidden, sigmoid output — with the data laid out as the maths has it: **X is (n_features × m_samples)**, one example per column. That convention is why every weight matrix multiplies from the left and why a transpose shows up at the usage line. It is the opposite of the (batch, features) layout PyTorch uses, and mixing the two is the single most common source of a shape error in a hand-written network.

items.label: X - input, one example per column

d.title: XOR, from chance to certainty
d.caption: Epoch 0's loss of 0.7992 is **above** ln 2 = 0.6931 — the loss of predicting 0.5 everywhere — because the random initial weights are confidently wrong on some of the four examples, which costs more than having no opinion. Accuracy is 100% by epoch 500 and everything after that is the loss sharpening predictions it already gets right, from 0.0485 down to 0.0015.

d.title: Two moons, and a plateau worth recognising
d.caption: Accuracy sits at 86.3% from epoch 1,000 to 3,000 while the loss creeps down — the network has found the roughly linear boundary that separates most of each crescent and is refining its confidence in it rather than its shape. Then between 3,000 and 4,000 something breaks: the loss drops from 0.2862 to 0.1768 and accuracy jumps to 93.3%. **That is the moment the boundary becomes curved.** A flat accuracy curve with a falling loss is not a stalled run; it is a run about to move.

d.title: The gradient check, and why the curves do not replace it
d.caption: Training curves say the gradients point downhill; they do not say the gradients are *right*. A backward pass with a transposed matrix or a missing 1/m can still train — badly, and in a way nothing reports. Comparing against autograd gives agreement to **2.98e-09 and 9.06e-09** in float64, and the residual is the 1e-08 clamp inside the logs that the NumPy loss has and the `dZ2 = A2 − Y` shortcut ignores. That is the definitive check, and it takes one run.

nodes.label: But not that it is correct
Run it once, before trusting anything

d.title: The problem both frameworks are given
d.caption: A binary classifier on a table: 569 tumours, 30 measured features, malignant or benign. Splitting it three ways — 400 to train, 69 to validate, 100 held back — is what makes the comparison honest, because the validation set is what the callbacks and the schedule react to and the test set is therefore the only clean number. The 62.7% positive rate also sets the baseline: an accuracy below that is worse than answering 'benign' every time.

d.title: Keras: every callback did its job in nineteen epochs
d.caption: The run stops itself. Validation loss bottoms out around epoch 9 at 0.1261; `ReduceLROnPlateau` halves the rate to 5.00e-04 after five epochs without improvement; `EarlyStopping` ends the run at 19 and restores the best weights. Note the shape of it — training loss keeps falling to 0.0344 while validation loss **rises** to 0.1611. That divergence is overfitting, and the callbacks are what stop it costing anything.

d.title: PyTorch: the same model, and the cost of no early stopping
d.caption: The loop runs the full hundred epochs on the cosine schedule, and the validation loss shows what that costs: it bottoms near epoch 9 at 0.1512 and then drifts up to 0.2203 by epoch 49 before the decaying rate pulls it back to 0.1846. **Eighty of the hundred epochs were spent getting back to where epoch 9 already was.** The test accuracy matches Keras at 0.9600 — the difference is not the framework, it is that one run stopped itself and the other did not.

d.title: The same eight decisions, made in two places
d.caption: Every row is one thing Keras decides for you and PyTorch hands back. None of them is hidden in Keras in a way you cannot override, and none is hard in PyTorch — but the two middle rows are where the bugs live, because `model.eval()` and the with-logits convention are silent when you get them wrong: dropout stays on during validation, or a sigmoid gets applied twice.
